label: AQ 0040
title: The zero that still changed its mind

questions.q: If the forward pass is deterministic, why does the server look random to me?
questions.a: The Thinking Machines post explains that the server is deterministic given all its requests, but other users' requests aren't your input: they set the batch size, which changes how the kernels add up your numbers, so your logits can differ run to run.

teach.title: How it works: the two halves

questions.q: Should every agent run on batch-invariant kernels?
questions.a: Only where bit-identical output is worth the cost: replaying a bug or research comparisons, say (our advice). In the Thinking Machines test, 1,000 short replies from Qwen3-8B took 42 s with their still unoptimised batch-invariant kernels against 26 s by default.

teach.title: How it works: the two halves

questions.q: How would you make the tool choice reliable rather than just repeatable?
questions.a: Check each call against the tool's schema and the user's request before running it, log the full input of every run, and measure how often the agent picks the right tool across varied inputs. A deterministic wrong answer is still wrong.

teach.title: How it works: the two halves

questions.q: Why can greedy decoding give different outputs for the same prompt on a busy server?
questions.a: The batch size changes how the GPU kernels split their sums, and floating-point addition rounds differently in different orders. The logits shift slightly, enough to flip a near-tie between two tokens.

A kernel property: it adds numbers in the same order whatever the batch size, so one request's result doesn't depend on what else runs with it. Thinking Machines needed it for RMSNorm, matrix multiplication and attention.

questions.q: Why is temperature 0 only half a fix even on a perfectly deterministic server?
questions.a: It makes the choice repeatable, not correct: if the model slightly prefers the wrong tool, greedy decoding picks that wrong tool every time.
